headline: The Easy Part of Coding Got Automated. The Judgment Part Didn't.
summary: AI can generate code quickly, but it often requests overly broad permissions, shifting the burden of secure configuration to human developers. This makes code review, especially for security, more complex and time-consuming.
details: AI can generate code, like a Lambda function, in mere seconds. However, it frequently requests overly broad permissions, such as s3:* or dynamodb:* with wildcard resources, without understanding the principle of least privilege.

This shifts the critical responsibility to the developer to meticulously refine security policies and ensure safe operation. The author noted spending significantly more time narrowing down IAM policies than the AI took to write the entire function.

The core shift is that while code generation has become cheap, the cost and complexity of code review, particularly for security and proper scoping, have increased. Knowing what 'good' and secure code looks like remains a critical human skill that AI has yet to master.

headline_marked: [[NeoGeo AES+ console delayed to late 2027]] due to AI-driven RAM crunch
headline: NeoGeo AES+ console delayed to late 2027 due to AI-driven RAM crunch
summary: Plaion's hardware-accurate replica of the classic NeoGeo console will now arrive on September 16, 2027, with the delay attributed to the ongoing global memory shortage and higher-than-expected demand.
details: Plaion's NeoGeo AES+, a 1:1 hardware replica of SNK's classic console, has been delayed by 10 months. The new release date is set for September 16, 2027. This delay is primarily due to the global AI-driven RAM shortage, compounded by higher-than-anticipated demand for the console.

Unlike most modern console re-releases that rely on software emulation, the AES+ is designed to be an exact, 100% compatible replica through physical hardware. Plaion is utilizing dedicated ASIC chips and contemporary clones of original processors like the Motorola 68000 and Zilog Z80A.

The development team includes Jotego, a long-time MiSTER core developer, ensuring the project's authenticity. The console will even use 5V power delivery for direct compatibility with original NeoGeo AES cartridges.

The AES+ is expected to work with every game cartridge from the original NeoGeo AES home console. Modern third-party adapters will also allow the use of original arcade cartridges. Plaion is re-releasing ten iconic games in cartridge form, including Metal Slug and King of Fighters 2002.

The original NeoGeo was unique for using the same hardware in both home and arcade versions, a first for its time. It also introduced memory cards for save games and came with a serious arcade joystick, delivering on the promise of "arcade-quality games in your home."

The original AES was a premium product, costing $399.99 at launch in 1990 (over $1,000 in today's money) for the base system. The Gold package, with two sticks, a game, and a memory card, was $649.99 (over $1,600 today).

The console's longevity stemmed from its overpowered architecture, featuring seven processors and co-processors, and a GPU with a 24-bit bus. It supported 3840 simultaneous colors across 380 sprites with hardware scaling.
Expandable storage was another key factor, with late-era cartridges storing up to 716 Mb (89.5 MB). The only notable omission was a direct-to-screen drawing mechanism, which limited certain ports.

The NeoGeo AES+ base model, including the console and one stick, will cost $249.99 (€199.99). The Anniversary Edition, with Metal Slug, a wireless joystick, and a memory card, is priced at $349.99 (€299.99). The Ultimate Edition, featuring ten games, two joysticks, and a gamepad, will be $999.99 (€899.99).
